title: Given the roots of two binary trees root and subRoot, return true if there is a subtree of root with the same structure and values as subRoot.
shortTitle: Subtree of Another Tree — recursive comparison at every node

s1_definition.profdef: Subtree of Another Tree checks whether a smaller tree appears exactly as a subtree somewhere inside a larger tree. The straightforward solution traverses the larger tree and, at each node, runs a same-tree comparison against the candidate subtree; if any node's subtree matches exactly in structure and values, the answer is true.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh has the full bank org chart and a small team chart, and he wants to know whether that exact team, same people in the same shape, appears anywhere inside the full chart. He walks the big chart, and at every manager he checks whether the team hanging below that manager matches the small chart exactly. If he finds one spot that matches completely, the answer is yes.
s1_definition.oneliner: At every node of the big tree, run a full same-tree check against the candidate; if any check passes, it is a subtree.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Subtree of Another Tree checks whether a smaller tree appears exactly as a subtree somewhere inside a larger tree. The straightforward solution traverses the larger tree and, at each node, runs a same-tree comparison against the candidate subtree; if any node's subtree matches exactly in structure and values, the answer is true.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Rajesh has the full bank org chart and a small team chart, and he wants to know whether that exact team, same people in the same shape, appears anywhere inside the full chart. He walks the big chart, and at every manager he checks whether the team hanging below that manager matches the small chart exactly. If he finds one spot that matches completely, the answer is yes.

**One line to remember:** At every node of the big tree, run a full same-tree check against the candidate; if any check passes, it is a subtree.

sections.s2_technical:
This problem composes two ideas: traversing the main tree, and at each stop performing an exact tree-equality check. The outer traversal picks candidate anchor points, and the inner check verifies an exact match from that anchor.

The outer method visits each node of the main tree. At each node it first checks whether the subtree rooted there is identical to the candidate. For example: `if (isSameTree(node, subRoot)) return true;`. If not, it recurses into the children, returning true if either side contains the subtree. For example: `return isSubtree(node.left, subRoot) || isSubtree(node.right, subRoot);`.

The inner same-tree check is the standard identical-trees comparison: both null means match, one null means mismatch, values must be equal, and both subtrees must match. For example: `return a.val == b.val && isSameTree(a.left, b.left) && isSameTree(a.right, b.right);`.

The time complexity is the product of the two tree sizes in the worst case, because each of the main tree's nodes may trigger a comparison that scans the whole candidate. For a main tree of size n and candidate of size m this is order n times m. The space is proportional to the combined heights from the recursion.

A senior nuance is the efficient alternative: serialize both trees into strings with explicit null markers, then check whether the candidate's serialization is a substring of the main tree's serialization, which with a linear-time string matcher like Knuth-Morris-Pratt gives order n plus m. You must use unambiguous delimiters and null sentinels so that, for example, a value of twelve is not confused with a one next to a two, and so that a smaller value is not falsely matched as a prefix of a larger node. Recognizing both the simple quadratic approach and the linear serialization approach, and the pitfalls of the latter, is the senior-level answer.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, the compliance team keeps a template of a known fraudulent approval pattern as a small tree, and they want to detect whether that exact pattern appears anywhere inside a branch's full approval hierarchy. This is exactly how Subtree of Another Tree works — searching for an exact smaller tree inside a larger one.

Problem 2 — The match must be exact in both structure and the role at each position, because a near-match is not the flagged pattern. This is exactly why the inner check is a strict same-tree comparison rather than a loose containment test.

The mini-project builds a `RoleNode` class, a `PatternMatchService` with the outer traversal and inner same-tree check plus logging, and a runnable demo that searches for a pattern that is present and one that is absent.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is the hierarchy rooted at Manager and the present pattern rooted at CreditOfficer with children Clerk and Verifier.

Step 1: The outer search starts at Manager. It runs the same-tree check between Manager's subtree and the pattern. Manager's role does not equal CreditOfficer, so the check fails. It recurses into Manager's children.

Step 2: It visits CreditOfficer. It runs the same-tree check between CreditOfficer's subtree and the pattern. CreditOfficer equals CreditOfficer, then the left children Clerk equal Clerk, then the right children Verifier equal Verifier, and all deeper children are null on both sides. The same-tree check returns true, so the subtree is found and the search returns true immediately.

Step 3: The service logs that the fraud pattern was detected as a subtree.

Step 4: For the absent pattern with children Clerk and Auditor, the search again reaches CreditOfficer and runs the same-tree check. CreditOfficer matches and Clerk matches on the left, but on the right Verifier does not equal Auditor, so the check fails. It then checks RiskHead and the leaf nodes, none of which match, so the overall result is false and the service logs that the pattern is not present.

```text
2026-10-26T19:20:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — Fraud Pattern Subtree Detection
2026-10-26T19:20:00Z [SEVERE] Fraud pattern DETECTED as a subtree — investigate
2026-10-26T19:20:00Z [INFO] Fraud pattern not present in this hierarchy
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Subtree of Another Tree composes two ideas: traversing the larger tree to pick candidate anchor points, and at each anchor running a strict same-tree comparison against the candidate subtree. The outer traversal visits every node of the main tree, and at each one I first check whether the subtree rooted there is exactly equal to the candidate in both structure and values. If it is, I return true; otherwise I recurse into both children and return true if either side contains the pattern.

The inner same-tree check is the standard identical-trees routine: both null is a match, exactly one null is a mismatch, values must be equal, and both subtrees must recursively match. Because the match must be exact, I use a strict equality rather than any loose containment, since a near-match is not the pattern I am looking for.

The naive complexity is the product of the two tree sizes, because each node of the main tree may trigger a comparison that scans the whole candidate. I always mention the efficient alternative: serialize both trees with explicit null markers and delimiters, then check whether the candidate's serialization is a substring of the main tree's serialization using a linear-time matcher like Knuth-Morris-Pratt, which gives linear total time. The delimiters and null sentinels are essential so that adjacent values are not confused and a smaller value is not falsely matched as a prefix.

In my project at National Bank of India, I used this in fraud-pattern detection. Compliance keeps a template of a known fraudulent approval pattern as a small tree, and we search for that exact pattern inside each branch's full approval hierarchy. The match must be exact in both shape and the role at each position, so the strict same-tree inner check is what prevents false positives, and when a branch is large with many patterns to scan, I switch to the serialization-plus-substring approach for linear performance.
